content:
Have you ever turned on the radio and felt like every pop song sounds the same? Or watched a horror movie and figured out the ending within 20 minutes?

Researchers from Singapore Management University and James Cook University Singapore published a new paper in *Frontiers in Psychology*, pointing out that "hyperselection" refers to how, under intense competition, humans are increasingly adept at identifying and optimising effective solutions, constantly selecting for the same traits rather than trying other options.

The result is a major blow to creativity. In an increasingly optimisation-driven world, "hyperselection" makes everything—from music and urban design to football matches—more homogeneous.

Lead author and research psychologist Jose C. Yong likens "hyperselection" to natural selection—the evolutionary process whereby individuals with advantageous traits or more effective strategies are more likely to survive and reproduce. Modern technology has made this selection process extremely rapid and intense.

Yong says: "We can now instantly identify the best performer, copy it almost immediately, and keep optimising. When selection pressure is high—such as when competition is fierce or failing to optimise has serious consequences—this process accelerates."

Optimisation is usually useful because it helps achieve goals more efficiently. But when everyone is optimising for the same goal, other traits, behaviours, products and strategies may disappear, with efficiency replacing 'diversity or variation—which might actually be more adaptive and useful.'"

When we fall into "hyperselection," we lose creative masterpieces like *Bohemian Rhapsody*.

When explaining the concept of "hyperselection" to those unfamiliar with it, [researchers] like to cite Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody." Critics in 1975 initially slammed the song as "audacious pastiche" and a "stylistic hodgepodge," but the single is now regarded as one of the greatest works in rock history, largely because the band dared to take them.

"*Bohemian Rhapsody* is the opposite of hyperselection."

Yong says: "The song is nearly six minutes long, spans dramatically different musical sections, has no traditional verse-chorus structure, and includes an operatic passage—it really stands out."

Another song that clearly isn't a product of "hyperselection" is Stevie Nicks's "Edge of Seventeen," which breaks conventional song structure and has a highly distinctive sonic quality. Yong also mentions System of a Down, describing their music as sounding "completely not of this world," yet still topping charts, "because their music was fresh and unique enough."

Compared with the past, pop songs played on radio today could be described as unoriginal and bland—to the point that Yong struggled to think of a single distinctive work to use as an illustration.

He says: "Honestly, I'm not sure I can point to a current pop song as an example of [the opposite of] 'hyperselection,' partly because so many pop songs today sound alike, and none leave a deep impression."

But he notes that certain music genres are perfect illustrations of "hyperselection." For example, the gloomy, melancholic pop songs where singers murmur softly, or the ubiquitous mumble-rap of a few years ago.

"Hyperselection" also explains why Yong's co-author and fellow research psychologist Edison Tan almost never listens to the radio anymore, instead seeking out newer indie artists with lower play counts.

Tan told *HuffPost*: "It's not that my taste has changed; the world has changed. I crave rich, nuanced emotional expression, and pop music can no longer provide it."

Yong notes that driven by metrics like streaming counts, market reach, and the fleeting attention spans of social media, music has become shorter and simpler—a trend well documented in the literature.

Beyond music, in what other fields does "hyperselection" appear?

Yong, Tan and co-author Simon S. Groome argue that "hyperselection"—the pursuit of optimisation and efficiency—has made nearly every aspect of life more predictable, formulaic and dull. They have observed the same phenomenon in sports.

In the world of professional football, teams are constantly searching for tactics that can give them an edge. Once a strategy proves effective, opponents quickly emulate it. Matches become more competitive and tactically sophisticated, but the way teams play is also growing increasingly similar, leaving less and less room for individual style to shine.

Professional careers are no exception. Tan uses academia, a world he knows well, as an example.

He says: "When we were in graduate school, we were taught to think boldly, explore new ideas, and understand how the world works."

In an ideal world, the best researchers should be the most creative problem-solvers—those who dare to be different. But reality falls far short of this ideal.

Tan says: "Scholars are forced to prove their worth through metrics like publication counts, citation numbers, and even the research funding they secure through grants, rather than being judged on the value of the ideas themselves."

He adds: "The 'P' in PhD stands for philosophy, and that meaning has long since vanished. When we see the same pattern repeating itself across all areas of life, we can't help but wonder whether some fundamental force is driving these trends."

Artificial intelligence will accelerate "hyperselection"

Yong believes that artificial intelligence will accelerate "hyperselection," which is almost self-evident. AI is itself designed to perform recursive optimisation with minimal human intervention, operating at speeds and scales far beyond what humans or previous technologies could achieve.

He says: "We're already seeing this in online content—AI-generated articles, ad copy, social media posts, images, films, web designs, even music. They all feel extremely similar because they're generated based on the same underlying patterns and constantly optimised for what works."

If people consume this content uncritically, there will be almost no countervailing force to resist AI-driven "hyperselection."

"Hyperselection" isn't entirely without merit, but creators should be mindful of this phenomenon.

Yong emphasises that optimisation itself is not wrong—it helps people achieve goals and improve lives. But because the pressure to optimise can be enormous, creators may unknowingly sacrifice adaptive diversity.

He says: "That's exactly why it's important to be aware that 'hyperselection' exists, and it's why I wanted to articulate this concept clearly—because once we can recognise it, we can think about how to respond when it appears."

Yong says the key is understanding how easily we fall into the "hyperselection" trap, and finding ways to cultivate creativity and preserve diversity.

He says: "Creativity often comes from exposure to different things, then combining them in new ways. If everything looks, sounds, and feels the same, we lose the treasure trove of alternative strategies and the raw material from which new ideas are born."

We also need to think more critically about the content we consume.

Yong says: "If audiences can recognise that music, films or other cultural products have become overly formulaic, and crave something more interesting, that in itself will change the selection pressures shaping production."
